quiz.title: Grade 1 Logical Reasoning Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight simple questions on patterns, sequences and odd-one-out, the same thinking skills Logiquids worksheets build. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What comes next? Circle, Square, Circle, Square, ___
questions.explanation: The shapes take turns: circle, square, circle, square. After a square it is the circle's turn again.

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out? Apple, Banana, Car, Mango
questions.explanation: Apple, banana and mango are all fruits you can eat. A car is not a fruit, so it does not belong.
The numbers go up by 2 each time: 2, 4, 6, then 8, then 10.

questions.q: Big, Bigger, ___. Which word completes it?
questions.explanation: The words show more and more size: big, bigger, biggest. This is a size sequence.

questions.q: A cat has 4 legs. How many legs do 2 cats have?
questions.explanation: Each cat has 4 legs. Two cats means 4 and 4 more, which is 8 legs in all.

questions.q: Which shape is different from the others? Red circle, Red circle, Blue circle, Red circle
questions.explanation: Three of the circles are red and one is blue. The blue circle is the one that is different.
The numbers count up one at a time: 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5 comes next.

questions.q: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, ___. Which day is next?
questions.explanation: The days go in order. After Tuesday comes Wednesday.

faq.q: What are Logiquids worksheets for Grade 1?
faq.a: Logiquids is a logical-reasoning worksheet programme for young children. For Grade 1 the sheets use pictures and simple numbers to practise patterns, sequences, odd-one-out and sorting, so a 6-year-old builds thinking skills alongside early maths.

faq.q: What skills do these worksheets build?
faq.a: They train the reasoning a child needs across every subject: spotting patterns, comparing sizes and quantities, grouping things that belong together, and working out what comes next. These are the habits behind confident problem-solving later on.

faq.q: Are logical-reasoning worksheets too hard for a 6-year-old?
faq.a: No, as long as they stay picture-based and short. A Grade 1 child handles odd-one-out and simple patterns happily; the trick is a few questions at a time rather than a long sheet, so it feels like a puzzle and not a test.

faq.q: How often should my child practise reasoning?
faq.a: About ten minutes a day works better than one long session on the weekend. Mix a pattern puzzle with a couple of counting questions so the child has to choose how to think, which is where real reasoning shows up.
